premise: The Nianduo section in the Nyalam area and the Wölong sec-tion in the Tingri area are located in the Tethyan Himalaya on the Kioto carbonate platform (Fig.1B).
Both sections have a con-tinuously exposed marine sedimentary succession ranging from the upper Lower Jurassic Pupuga Formation to the lower Mid-dle Jurassic Nieniexiongla Formation (Fig.2A–D).
The Pupuga For-mation represents a shallow-water carbonate platform dominated by grainstones/packstones deposited under high-energy conditions with occasional influxes of terrigenous material.

The lower-middle Pupuga Formation in both Tingri and Nyalam areas yields abundant and diversified benthic foraminifera including Haurania deserta, Or-bitopsella praecursor, Palaeomayncina termieri, Amijiella amiji, Cyclor-bitopsella tibetica, Ammobaculites sp., Lituosepta cf. compressa, Pseu-docyclammina cf. liasica(Jadoul et al., 1998;Wignall et al., 2006).

These foraminiferal assemblages of the Tibetan Himalaya are sim-ilar to those observed in the Liassic carbonate platforms of the SW Tethyan margin in the northern hemisphere, and indicate a late Sinemurian–late Pliensbachian age (BouDagher-Fadel, 2008).

In the upper Pupuga Formation, two intervals enriched in Lithi-otisbivalves respectively occur ∼20–30m and ∼3–4m below the boundary with the overlying Nieniexiongla Formation in both the Nianduo and Wölong sections (Figs.3and 4).

The overlying Nie-niexiongla Formation represents a middle/outer carbonate ramp environment, and is characterized by mudstones deposited under low-energy conditions intercalated with abundant coarse-grained beds (Han et al., 2016).

premise: The Op Zämer section exhibits Upper Pliensbachian strata corresponding to the Marnes d’Ottemt Formation (Fig. 2).
Facies consist of pale grey clayed sediments with an abundant macrofauna (belemnites, brachiopods, bivalves and ostracods).

Another prominent feature of this sedimentary unit, dated in the spinatum zone, is the considerable number of centimetric limonite nodules (from the base up to 80 cm in this section) and subsequent phosphate (apatite) nodules from 80 to 120 cm.
The sedimentary unit overlaying the Pliensbachian–Toarcian boundary consists of clayed orange facies in which no ammonite specimens were observed.
This level corresponds to the lower part of the Marnes à Semicelatum Formation, biostratigraphically assigned to the tenuicostatum zone in SE Belgium (Delsate, 1990; Boulvain et al., 2001).

The following unit consists of dark blue/grey calcareous claystone, typical of the Marnes à Semicelatum Formation with many belemnites and large carbonate nodules whose diameters comprise between 10 and 30 cm.
This 80 cm thick interval is assigned to the semicelatum sub-zone of the Early Toarcian.

The top of the Op Zämer section exhibits the Lower Toarcian black shales of the Schistes carton Formation (lithostratigraphically equivalent to the Jet Rock Formation in Yorkshire, or to the Posidonienschiefer Formation in SW Germany) that provide compelling evidence for supra-regional anoxia.
Black shales consist of very dark and finely laminated sediments, with very scarce macropalaeontological content (restricted to few ammonite specimens and Bositra spp. casts).
The contact between the Schistes carton lithology and the underlying pale grey marls is sharp and underpinned by many pluricentimetric wood fragments recovered in the Op Zämer section (Fig. 2).
In adjacent regions in Belgium, a thin sandy bed containing an abundant fish macrofauna has been reported at this transition (Delsate et al., 1999).

premise: The researchwas carried out at the La Cerradura (CE) section (Fig. 1A and B), located by the trench of motorway A-44, km 57 (37°41′47.8″N; 3°37′57.6″W).
The section is 15 km south of Jaén city (province of Jaén).
The CE section belongs to the External Subbetic (Betic External Zones; Fig. 1A and B).
The Betic External Zones comprise the Prebetic and Subbetic, bothmade up of thick successions of Triassic toMiocene strata (Vera, 2004).
The Prebetic rockswere deposited in shallowmarine shelf, coastal plain, and continental environments during the Jurassic and Cretaceous.
The Subbetic is a relatively distal setting, featuring pelagic swells with low subsidence and subsident central troughs during the Jurassic (Fig. 2).

Jurassic sedimentation in the External Subbetic is characterised by shallow shelf deposits in the lowermost Jurassic (Gavilán Fm, Fig. 1B and C), overlain by hemipelagic facies of marls and marly limestones (Fig. 1D), Pliensbachian–Aalenian in age (Zegrí Fm).

The main fragmentation stage of the large carbonate platform developed during the earliest Jurassic (García-Hernández et al., 1987, 1989; Vera, 2001, 2004), when the Gavilán Fm rocks were deposited, since the middle Pliensbachian.
Blocks were rotated along a number of listric faults (Vera, 2001).
Blocks less subsided became pelagic swells with condensed facies (e.g. Braga et al., 1981).
The blocks with differential subsidence resulted in remarkable thickness changes (Vera, 2004).
The rocks made up the Zegrí Fm in the La Cerradura section (Fig. 1D) were deposited in the subsident area with an expanded and continuous sedimentation (Braga, 1983; Jiménez, 1986).

Lithological inspection of the core indicates significant differences in sedimentation style and sediment composition be-tween the formations (Figs.2, S2).

The Grès médioliasiques Fm (31.97–39.92m; Interval 4) consists of homogeneouslight-grey to grey marls with minor contributions of silt, strongly affected by bioturbation and potentially by erosional events.

Detailed inspection reveals that these laminated sediments were frequently interrupted by intercalated horizons that show an indistinct lamination and a partly homogeneoussedimentation style, which indicate enhanced bioturbation and sediment rework-ing (Fig. S2).
Horizons with indistinct lamination are most pro-nounced in the lower part of the Schistes Carton Fm (Interval2).

The basal Schistes Carton Fm (30.75–31.97m; Interval 3) differs from the upper part, as this interval shows the lowest carbonate content (Fig.2) and thus rather represents bituminous claystones (black shale, sensu lato) than bituminous marls.

The borehole provided a continuous recovery of core-samples from the Triassic to the Upper Jurassic.
The studied K2-5 core section is 9 m long, sampling an interval from 1037.10 to 1028.10 m depth (with respect to ground level datum), and comprises Lower Toarcian sediments.

The lithology of the basal Toarcian (Tenuicostatum Zone) is represented by marine calcareous sandstones with abundant detrital quartz (Middle Liassic sandstones), followed by marls and calcareous marls (containing several organic-rich and laminated intervals, making up the “Schistes carton” formation) assigned to the Serpentinum Zone (Fig. 2).

premise: The Wölong section analyzed in this study (Fig.1B; 28°29′2″ N, 87°02′3″ E) is located in the southern zone of the Tibetan Tethys Himalaya.

The Lower Jurassic has been well constrained in the section by larger benthic foraminifera, the occurrence of Lithio-tisbivalves, and chemostratigraphy (Jadoul et al., 1998; Han et al., 2016, 2018, 2021).

At Wölong, the following lithostratigraphic units are exposed (from the bottom to the top): the Zhamure Formation (upper Sinemurian–lower Pliensbachian), the Pupuga Formation (upper Pliensbachian–lowest Toarcian) and the Nieniex-iongla Formation (Toarcian–Aalenian?).

Overall, the succession il-lustrates an evolution that sees a progressive decrease in the ter-rigenous content of the sediments and an increase of carbonate-rich sediment through time (Jadoul et al., 1998; Han et al., 2016, 2021): (1) The lower Zhamure Formation mainly documents a bar-rier island-lagoon environment, characterized by mixed carbonate–siliciclastic deposits; (2) the overlying Pupuga Formation grad-ually passes up-section into shallow-water platform carbonates, dominated by bioclastic grainstones/packstones and yielding Lithi-otisbivalves; (3) the Nieniexiongla Formation represents a deeper carbonate ramp and is mainly composed of micrites alternating with coarser grained storm-generated layers.

The carbon-isotope record from the Wölong section has revealed a series of pertur-bations that can be correlated with the Sinemurian–Pliensbachian boundary event (SPBE), the margaritatuszone event (ME) and margaritatus–spinatumboundary event (MSBE) (Fig.2; Han et al., 2021).

premise: The Dawen section is located in the interior of the Great Bank of Guizhou, one in a series of isolated carbonate platforms in the Nanpanjiang Basin, South China (Fig. 1).

The Nanpanjiang Basin was situated south and east of the mainly carbonate Yangtze Platform and formed a deep-marine embayment into the platform that opened to the Tethys to the east and south during the Early Triassic.
The entire region resides on the South China Block, which was located in equatorial eastern Tethys during the Early Triassic (Tong and Yin, 2002).

The Great Bank of Guizhou initiated as patch reefs and open-marine skeletal-grainstone during a latest Permian deepening event and resultant expansion of the Nanpanjiang Basin, and continued aggrading until it was eventually drowned by siliciclastic turbidites during the Late Triassic (Lehrmann et al., 1998; Enos et al., 1998, 2006).

Previous studies provide detailed accounts of the stratigraphic architecture (Lehrmann et al., 1998, 2003, 2005a, 2005b), skeletal carbonate composition (Payne et al., 2006), and carbon isotopic evolution (Krull et al., 2004; Payne et al., 2004) of the platform, and therefore are addressed only briefly here.
At the Dawen section, strata spanning the Permian–Triassic transition consist of shallow-marine skeletal packstone of the upper Wujiaping Formation (Late Permian).
These packstones contain a diverse open-marine biota (Payne et al., 2006) and are overlain by  16 m of calcimicrobial framestone (microbialite) (Fig. 2).

The microbialite facies is capped by a microgastropod-rich skeletal- grainstone bed, which in turn is overlain conformably by a  60 m thick succession of carbonate mudstone of the Lower Triassic Daye Formation.

premise: The Daxiakou section (GPS: N31°06.8749′, E110°48.2099′) isis located 6 km east of Xiakou Town, in Xingshan County, western Hubei Province, South China (Fig. 1).
Here, Permian and Triassic successions are fairly complete and well exposed along roadcuts of the Yichang- Chongqing highway.
Paleogeographically, the Xiaokou area was situated in an offshore to shelf basin setting on the northern margin of the Middle Yangtze Platform during the P–Tr transition (Feng et al., 1997).
The uppermost Permian comprises the Wuchiaping and Dalong formations.
The former is composed of medium-bedded muddy limestone, whereas the latter unit consists of black mudstone and siliceous shale with minor interbeds of muddy limestone.

The Dalong Formation is widely distributed in South China and has been interpreted as the result of sedimentation in shelf basins located between carbonate platforms during the latest Permian (Chen et al., 2010, 2011).
The Lower Triassic succession is composed of the Daye and Jialingjiang formations.

The former is characterized by alternations of calcareous mudstone and thin-bedded muddy limestone in the lower part and thin-bedded to thick dolomitic limestone and dolomite in the upper part, while the latter formation comprises thick-bedded limestone.
The Daye Formation represents deposition in carbonate ramp to pertidal settings, whereas the Jialingjiang Formation represents a carbonate platform setting (Tong et al., 2007).
The PTB at Daxiakou was placed at the base of the Daye Formation (Wang and Xia, 2004; Zhao et al., 2013; Fig. 2).

The Daxiakou succession not only yields the same conodont zones as those recorded in Meishan (Wang and Xia, 2004; Zhao et al., 2005c), but also contains volcanic ash beds that are correlative with their counterparts from the Meishan GSSP (Jiang et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2009).
Bivalve assemblages from the Daye and Jialingjiang Formations point collectively to a Griesbachian–Smithian and Spathian age, respectively (Li et al., 2009).

premise: The Shangsi section is located about 1 km north of the Shangsi Village, Guangyuan City, Sichuan Province, and its sequence is very well exposed along the Changjianggou Creek.
The section was located in the eastern Paleotethys and near the paleoequator during the Lopingian, and was previously assigned to the Equatorial Warm Water Province (EWWP; Mei and Henderson, 2001).
Sediments were deposited in a slope to basinal setting on the northwest margin of the South China Block during the Lopingian (Fig. 1).
Although strata of the entire Permian are well exposed here, this study mainly focuses on the Wuchiaping, Talung and the base of the Feixianguan formations.
The Wuchiaping Formation is subdivided into the Wangpo Shale at the base and the main part comprising limestone.

The Wangpo Shale is composed of limonite, silty mudstone, coal and ash beds, and is up to 2m thick; it was deposited and exposed during the lowstand that led to the development of a major unconformity in many other regions (Mei, 1995; Mei and Shi, 1999; Mei et al., 1999; Shi et al., 1999).
Most of the Wuchiaping Formation is composed of medium- to thick-bedded limestone with cherty nodules.
The Talung Formation consists of thin-bedded limestone with cherty nodules in the lower part, organic-rich limestone in the middle part, and siliceous limestone with many ash beds in the upper part.

The basal Feixianguan Formation is composed of calcareous mudstone interbedded with argillaceous limestone in the basal part, followed by thin-bedded limestone with debris flow deposits higher in the section.

premise: The Dajiang section is located in Bianyang Town, Luodian County, Guizhou Province, China.
Due to the continuous record and good exposure of the PTB strata, the Dajiang section is ideal for investigating shallow water platform facies.

As a result of the eruption of the Emeishan basalt and the formation of related basement fractures during the late Permian, the northern margin of the Yangtze Platform exhibits an apparent paleogeographic pattern of platform–platform margin– basin, with some isolated carbonate platforms within the platform margin and basin zones.

The Nanpanjing Basin was located on the southern margin of the Yangtze Platform, and the isolated carbonate platform, which was located on the southern margin of the Nanpanjing Basin, is called the Great Bank of Guizhou (Lehrmann et al., 1998, 2005).
The Dajiang section was located on the interior of the Great Bank of Guizhou (Fig. 1b), and the water depth was <20–30 m (Lehrmann et al., 1998).

The stratigraphic sequence of the Dajiang section, from bottom to top, consists of bioclastic limestone of the Upper Permian Wujiaping Formation and massive microbialite and thin- to medium-bedded limestone of the Lower Triassic Daye Formation (Fig. 1d).

premise: The Cabin Fork study area is located in the southeastern Bighorn Basin of Wyoming (Fig. 1).
The Paleocene–Eocene transition is recorded in the lowest Willwood Formation.

Locally the underlying Fort Union Formation is about 110 m thick, rests unconformably on Cretaceous strata, and consists of gray to grayish-yellow mudstones, carbonaceous shales (3–40% TOC), mostly fine-grained sandstones, and rare coals near its base (Bown, 1980; Wing, 1998).

The mudstones, shales and coal represent deposition on low-lying floodplains, and the sandstones have bedding features and geometries consistent with deposition in fluvial channels or channel margins.
Fossil plants and mammals show that all of the FortUnion Formation in the study area is late Paleocene in age (Wing, 1998; Wing et al., 2005).

The variegated mudstones represent paleosols formed on fine, overbank deposits; the lenticular shale bodies were deposited in abandoned channels; and the sandstones represent channel or channel-margin settings (Bown, 1980; Wing, 1998).

premise: ODP Leg 174AX Millville core recovered the Vincentown, Marlboro, and Manasquan Formations (257.55–280.33 m) that span the Paleocene/Eocene boundary (Figure 3).
The Vincentown Formation is a micaceous, glauconitic, sandy silt at Millville.
The contact between the Vincentown and Marlboro Formations occurs within a 0.6 ft transition zone with decreasing upward glauconite and coarse fraction content.
Clayey silts (mean grain size 8 μm) of the Marlboro Formation comprise an expanded CIE “core” (10m thick) at Millville.
The CIE recovery interval (5.5m thick) captures a lithologic transition from the Marlboro Formation to coarser informal units referred to as A and B here (discussed in the supporting information).
The post-CIE section consists of glauconitic, carbonate-rich sandy silts of the Manasquan Formation overlying unit B above an unconformity at 258.09 m.
For more information on lithostratigraphy and paleowater depth estimates, see the supporting information.

premise: During the Paleocene and early Eocene, Tingri (south Tibet) was located in the Tethyan Himalaya of the northern Greater Indian continental margin (Fig. 2), where thick carbonate sequences of the Zhepure Shan Formation were deposited on a tropical carbonate ramp (Willems et al., 1996; Zhang et al., 2013).

To the south of the Tethyan Himalaya, contemporary shallow marine strata of the Subathu Formation crops out in the Lesser Himalaya (Najman, 2006), indicating that the southern shoreline of the Neo-Tethyan Ocean was located either within the Lesser Himalaya or even to the south.

By taking into account the post-55 Ma shortening of the upper crust in the Himalaya (DeCelles et al., 2002), Tingri was at least ~300kmaway from the shoreline during the PETM. The carbonate rocks of the Zhepure Shan Formation comprise four lithological members (Members A to D; Fig. 3a), the upper three of which are rich in larger benthic foraminifera.
Based on the larger foraminifera, ten Shallow Benthic Zones (SBZ) were distinguished in the Zhepure Shan Formation (Zhang et al., 2013).
Integration of bio- and chemostratigraphy enabled identification of the Paleocene-Eocene (P/ E) boundary within a nodular limestone in the upper part of the Member C (Zhang et al., 2013) (Fig. 3b).

We studied two parallel sections (10/11TM and 13ZS), at a distance of ~50m, in order to test for lateral consistency of the δ13Ccarb variations and evaluate the effect of mixed different components on the δ13Ccarb records.
hypothesis: Zhepure Shan Formation has the lithology carbonate.
head_type: Zhepure Shan Formation is a Strata.

premise: The Minervois is located in Southern France (Fig. 1A).
The transgressive early Eocene sediments directly overlie the Paleozoic basement of the „Montagne Noire“, forming a distinct angular unconformity (Plaziat, 1972).

Detailed stratigraphic logging in a 10 km wide area around Minerve (Fig. 1B) led to the investigation of a 290 m thick composite section, consisting of five sedimentary units (Fig. 2) in ascending order: (1) the Alveoline Limestone unit: ~ 42 m-thick white to blue-grey, alveoline -rich marine limestones with centimetric to decametric marls interbeds.
This marine unit rests on continental „Sparnacian“ deposits north of Fauzan; (2) the Blue Marl unit: 4 m of marine greenish to bluish marls, which are devoid of macrofossils.

The transition between the Alveoline Limestone and the Blue Marl units is marked by a ~ 80cm-thick oysterrich sandstone bed; (3) the Ventenac Limestone unit: ~ 73 m of beige to ochre lacustrine limestones with interbedded bioclastic calcareous marls.
Main biofacies consists of ostracods, gastropods, arthropod fragments and charophyte gyrogonites.
Lacustrine lithofacies is highlighted by numerous centimetric lignite beds, root traces and wavy or irregular interbeds.

The lowermost part of the Ventenac Limestone unit yielded the mammal locality of Fournes; (4) the Assignan Molasse unit: ~ 70 m-thick alternation of centimetric to metric coarse to fine fluvial sandstone lenses with intercalated ochre to pinkish marls and/or clays.

The Sainte-Eulalie mammal locality is located in the upper part of the Assignan Molasse unit; (5) the Agel Limestone unit: ~ 80 m of white to greyish lacustrine limestones, intercalated with centimetric to decimetric calcareous marls and centimetric lignitic beds, poor in bioclast content except for some ostracods or charophytes.
The Agel Marly Limestone unit yielded the Azillanet mammal locality.

premise: The Dababiya GSSP is located at the eastern side of the upper Nile Valley 35 km southeast of Luxor City (25°30′N, 32°31′E; Fig. 1, Dupuis et al., 2003; khozyem et al., 2014).
Although a number of studies have concentrated on outcrops in the Dababiya area (Dupuis et al., 2003; Schulte et al., 2011, 2013), the GSSP section was never before sampled systematically.
The reason is highly restricted access because of the limited outcrop exposure and fear that sampling would deplete the section.
As a result permission for sampling the GSSP was routinely denied.

We obtained permission by proposing to leave the GSSP in tact and instead sample one stratigraphic sequence 25 m to the east (Dababiya E) of the GSSP exposure and the other 50 m northwest (Dababiya NW, Fig. 1).
This sampling strategy is advantageous because the GSSP is in the deepest part of a submarine channel with variable erosion on either Fig. 1. side.

The two sections sampled ensure that the maximum available sediment deposition and variation in erosion and depositional patterns through the channel can be evaluated and compared with the already published GSSP record (Dupuis et al., 2003).

The Paleocene-Eocene transition in the southern margin of the Tethys in Egypt includes the outer-shelf deposits of northeastern Egypt and Sinai (i.e. Wadi Nukhul, Speijer and Wagner, 2002; Khozyem et al., 2013).

In the eastern desert the monocline of the Upper Cretaceous to Upper Eocene resulted in uplift and exposure of the outer shelf to marginal marine strata across the desert in northeastern Egypt where they are exposed in mesas and ridges (Aubry et al., 2007).
The Dababiya GSSP is one of these exposures.

Exposures in the Dababiya area consist of four lithostratigraphic formations as follows from older to younger (Fig. 2): Dakhla Shale Formation (greenish calcareous shale), Tarawan Formation (marly limestone to chalk), Esna Shale (greenish gray to dark gray shale), and the Thebes Formation (limestone and flint).
The Esna Shale Formation is divided into three main units (Esna-1, Esna-2 and Esna-3) based on carbonate contents (Dupuis et al., 2003).
Only Esna-1 and Esna-2 are exposed at the GSSP NW and E outcrops (Fig. 1, 2).
hypothesis: Dakhla Shale Formation has the lithology greenish calcareous shale.

premise: The Yangou Quarry section (117◦20′59.6472′′ N, 29◦11′ 39.4764′′ E) is located in the Yangou Coal Yard along Highway S205, which is near Yongshan Town and ~30 km northeast of Leping City, Jiangxi Province (Fig. 1).
This section consists of 13.5 m of strata exposed in a nearly vertical quarry face.

During the Permian-Triassic transition, this succession accumulated on an isolated carbonate bank close to the northern margin of the Yangtze Platform, recording inner shelf to tidal flat facies within the euphotic zone (Zhu, 1999; Song et al., 2012).
The Yangou Quarry section is not the same as the nearby (< 500 distant) “Yangou section” of earlier studies (Song et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2014).

Despite these two sections having been deposited within a few hundred meters of each other, they differ appreciably with regard to lithologies, conodont assemblages, and CIE patterns (see Sections 4–6), possibly due to deposition on different parts of an oolitic bank.
The Yangou section records the uppermost Permian to Lower Triassic Changxing Formation and the Lower Triassic Daye Formation.

The Changxing Formation is composed of dark grey, thick-bedded, locally argillaceous limestones yielding abundant shallow-water foraminifera such as Palaeofusulina, Nankinella and Reichelina, and algae such as Permocalculus, Gymnocodium, and Pseudovermiporella (Zhu et al., 1994).
The Daye Formation is composed of dark grey, medium- to thin-bedded, locally argillaceous limestones, occasionally interbedded with mudstones.

The fossil biotas are rich and well-studied in the Yangou area, including 23 species in three genera of conodonts (Sun et al., 2012), 15 genera of gastropods, 14 species in 11 genera of ostracods (Zhu, 1999), 39 species in 27 genera of foraminifera, and 4 species in7 genera of fusulinids (Tian et al., 2014).
Oolitic layers were previously reported from the uppermost Changxing Formation within the H. changxingensis Zone immediately above the EPME horizon (Sun et al., 2012; Tian et al., 2014).

Well-bedded dark micritic limestones with intercalated thin grainstone layers are developed at the base of the sampled section (Khachik Formation, Fig. 4A).

The transition to the overlying irregularly bedded to nodular gray and reddish limestones of the Akhura Formation is characterized by an irregular wavy surface with thin shaly/silty bands indicating potential submarine erosion and thus comprising a major stratigraphic gap (Baud et al., 1989).

Above the Boundary Clay, the basal part of the Karabaglyar Formation is represented by microbial stromatolitic as well as thrombolithic limestones (Fig. 2B) showing well-developed domal structures (Baud et al., 1997, 2007; Friesenbichler et al., 2018).

premise: The studied fauna is located at the uppermost Permian succession of the Shaiwa section, about 18 km northwest of the Houchang town of Ziyun County, Guizhou Province, South China (Fig. 1).

During the MiddleLate Permian, the Ziyun area lay in the Youjiang aulacogen, a south-north directed tectonic setting formed as the result of intra-plate rifting of the South China block during the late Late Palaeozoic Era (Luo et al . 1988; Yin et al . 1999).
This aulacogen became a deep-water trough or bathyal zone during the Changhsingian (Yin et al . 1999; see also Fig. 1).
In this setting the Shaiwa Group was deposited, and the sequence is today well exposed at the Shaiwa section.

premise: The Zhejue section is located between the 851 and 852 km markers of the national highway between Xuanwei City and Weining County, where the PTB succession is well-exposed (Fig. 1).
The upper Xuanwei Formation consists mainly of mudstone, sandstone, and siltstone interbedded with coal seams.
This interval contains abundant fossil plants, including Lobatannularia, Gigantopteris, Fascipteris, Stigmaria spp., Gigantoclea, Compsopteris, and Euestheria gutta (Yu et al., 2015).

The lower Kayitou Formation is composed mainly of siltstone, shale, and claystone, and it has yielded minor fossil plant fragments such as Lepidopteris sp. and Peltaspermum sp. The lithofacies and fossil plant types of the Zhejue section are consistent with a swampy (paludal) depositional setting such as a poorly drained floodplain (Yu et al., 2015).
hypothesis: Zhejue section includes the strata Xuanwei Formation.

premise: The roadcut at Daxiakou in South China is a superb exposure of the entire Induan through lower Olenekian stages of the Early Triassic (approximately 3 myr spanning 252 to 249 Ma).
The Daxiakou section is located 6 km east of Xiakou town in the Three Gorges area, Xingshan County, Yichang City, Hubei Province (transect from 31°6.837′N, 110°48.275′E to 31°6.920′N, 110°48.147′E).

These deposits on the lower slope of the Yangtze carbonate platform recorded climatic and sea-level changes in several ways, including varying proportions of carbonate to clay-silt, rock density, resistance to weathering, rock color, bottom-water oxidation, bioturbation and other characteristics (Li et al., 2016a,b; Wu et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2013).
The Lower Triassic Daye Formation in this setting consists mainly of thin beds of grayishwhite limestone that are rhythmically interbedded with marls and gray silty claystone (Fig. 1).
There is no evidence for gravity flow deposits, hiatuses or major bioturbation mixing of the thin beds during the Induan at Daxiakou.

The section has yielded high-resolution zonations from conodonts (Zhao et al., 2013) and bivalves (Li et al., 2009), carbon isotope stratigraphy (Tong et al., 2007), and analysis of Milankovitch cycles (Li et al., 2016a,b; Wu et al., 2012).
The color change of conodont fossils caused by thermal alteration of conodont fossils can be used to estimate the maximum temperature reached by a sedimentary rock (Epstein et al., 1977).
The conodont color alteration index at Daxiakou, which is pale brown to dark brown (Zhao et al., 2013), suggests a 50–140 °C temperature range (Epstein et al., 1977).

Some paleoclimate proxies may have a different sensitivity to diagenetic alteration; nevertheless, this conodont color alteration index indicates that intense thermal-induced diagenesis at Daxiakou was not significant.

premise: The studied material comes from the Mahmudia Quarry (45°03012.41″N, 29°03034.52″E), which is located in the Caeracul Mare Hill area, south of the village of Mahmudia, 35 km east of Tulcea (Fig. 1A, B).
The Middle Triassic Caerace Formation that is exposed in this limestone quarry can be subdivided into the Stromatactis-Limestone Member and the Tubiphytes- Limestone Member (Figs 1C, 2).
The latter is exposed in the northeastern part of the quarry and represents a Tubiphytes-microbial buildup that was first documented by Dobre-Popa (2011) and Popa et al. (2014).

It yields a rich macroinvertebrate fauna consisting of coiled nautiloids, ammonoids, bivalves, gastropods, brachiopods, sponges and crinoids (Popa et al. 2014; Forel & Gr adinaru 2018; N€utzel et al. 2018; Gr adinaru & Gaetani 2019).

The ammonoids found in the Tubiphytes-Limestone Member can be correlated with the Bithynian (early middle Anisian) Osmani-ammonoid Zone of the Northwestern Caucasus (Shevyrev 1995) and the lower part of the middle Anisian, that is, the Hyatti-ammonoid Zone of northwestern Nevada (Silberling & Nichols 1982; Bucher 1992; Monnet & Bucher 2006).
The Tubiphytesmicrobial buildup is a massive carbonate buildup without well-expressed bedding and consists of several different carbonate facies (Popa et al. 2014).
Among these are frequent packages of microbially mediated cement crusts, which were generated by syndepositional microbial mats.

These microbial mats and their cement crusts provided taphonomic conditions that were favourable for the preservation of minute details of the ornamentation of fossil shells and the primary colour patterns of some gastropods (Popa et al. 2014; Forel & Gr adinaru 2018; N€utzel et al. 2018).

So far, little has been published on the Triassic bivalves from the North Dobrogea Orogen (Peters 1867; Kittl 1908; Simionescu 1908, 1910a, b, 1911, 1925; Mir auț a & Iordan 1982; Mir auț a et al. 1984), making the present work a significant contribution to the knowledge of the bivalve fauna from this Tethyan-type Triassic development.

premise: The Zhuqiao Section is located next to the Zhuqiao hydropower station, 2 km north of Zhuqiao village, Wufeng County, Yichang City, western Hubei Province, South China (Fig. 2).
The exposed strata at the Zhuqiao Section include the Late Permian Wuchiaping and Dalong formations, and the Early Triassic Daye Formation (Fig. 3).
The top of Wuchiaping Formation is composed of grey, dolomitic limestone with bed thicknesses of more than 1 m.

Dalong Formation consists of grey to dark grey thin-bedded siliceous mudstone and carbonaceous mudstone with a few interbeds of dark grey medium- to thin-bedded limestone, forming rhythmic stratification, and with welldeveloped thin laminations.
Planktonic or nektonic fossils including ammonoids and radiolarians are common in the thinbedded siliceous mudstone.
Thus, predominately siliceous facies of Dalong Formation at Zhuqiao are considered deep-water basin facies and belong to the mudstone of siliceous rock type (Niu et al., 2000).
Daye Formation consists of mudstone and muddy limestone with thin-bedded claystone.

premise: The Jiucaichong section is located between the 832 and 833 km markers of the national highway from Xuanwei City to Weining County, ~20 km north of the Zhejue section.

premise: The Upper Permian to Lower Triassic Yinkeng Formation is widely distributed throughout the Yangtze Block, South China, and conformably overlies Permian carbonate platform deposits (Liao, 1984; Yin et al., 2001).

premise: The Gabbs and Sunrise Formations in the Gabbs Valley Range (38°28' to 38°29" N, 118°04' to 118°05' W) comprise one of the best-studied conformable and fossiliferous marine sedimentary sequences spanning the latest Triassic and Early Jurassic (Fig. 1).
The paleogeographic setting was a back-arc basin between northwest Pangea and an accreting island chain, the remnant of the Triassic Havalla Basin (Taylor et al. 1983; Wyld et al. 2001).
The Gabbs Formation records the full final stage of the Triassic (Rhaetian) and the transition to the Jurassic (Hettangian).
The lower Sunrise Formation records the first few million years of the Jurassic (Hettangian and lower Sinemurian).

High chronostratigraphic and chronometric resolution is provided by analysis of conodonts (Orchard et al. 2007), ammonoids (Guex 1995), U/Pb tuff zircons (Schoene et al. 2010), and carbon and strontium isotopes (Guex et al. 2004; Ward et al. 2007; Guex et al. 2009; Bartolini et al. 2012; Tackett et al. 2014).

Ammonoid occurrences frame the mass extinction interval as the final 70–300 kyr of the Triassic, recorded in the uppermost Gabbs Formation (Guex et al. 2004; Lucas and Tanner 2007; Schoene et al. 2010; Bartolini et al. 2012).

Additional paleontology and paleoecology include faunal lists and abundance counts (Muller and Ferguson 1939; Laws 1982; Taylor et al. 1983; Taylor and Guex 2002; Tackett and Bottjer, in press; Ritterbush et al. 2014; Hodges and Stanley 2015).

The paleogeographic setting was a back-arc basin between northwest Pangea and an accreting island chain, the remnant of the Triassic Havalla Basin (Taylor et al. 1983; Wyld et al. 2001).
The Gabbs Formation records the full final stage of the Triassic (Rhaetian) and the transition to the Jurassic (Hettangian).
The lower Sunrise Formation records the first few million years of the Jurassic (Hettangian and lower Sinemurian).

High chronostratigraphic and chronometric resolution is provided by analysis of conodonts (Orchard et al. 2007), ammonoids (Guex 1995), U/Pb tuff zircons (Schoene et al. 2010), and carbon and strontium isotopes (Guex et al. 2004; Ward et al. 2007; Guex et al. 2009; Bartolini et al. 2012; Tackett et al. 2014).

Ammonoid occurrences frame the mass extinction interval as the final 70–300 kyr of the Triassic, recorded in the uppermost Gabbs Formation (Guex et al. 2004; Lucas and Tanner 2007; Schoene et al. 2010; Bartolini et al. 2012).

Additional paleontology and paleoecology include faunal lists and abundance counts (Muller and Ferguson 1939; Laws 1982; Taylor et al. 1983; Taylor and Guex 2002; Tackett and Bottjer, in press; Ritterbush et al. 2014; Hodges and Stanley 2015).

premise: The Lung Cam section is located near Lung Cam village, Ha Giang Province, Vietnam, about 10 km south of the Chinese border (23°14′30″N; 105°13′20″E).

Approximate placement of the LPME is facilitated by the carbonate δ13C profile, which exhibits a gradual decrease beginning ~1.2m below the formation contact, followed by an abrupt shift at the formation contact (Fig. 4; Song et al., 2007).
The presence of erosional surface(s) within the Lung Cam section has not been investigated in the field to date.

premise: At Bulla, the Permian–Triassic boundary is located in the Tesero Oolite.

premise: The Early Triassic Qinling Basin was a major seaway between the South China and Northern China blocks that narrowed to the east and opened to Paleo-Tethys in the west (Lai et al., 1992, 1995; Feng et al., 1994; Yin and Peng, 1995).
The studied Yiwagou Section was located in a shallow-water, carbonate platform at the northern margin of South China Block and on the southern side of the Basin (Fig. 1).
There has been little research in the region because of its inaccessibility and high altitude (but see Yin et al., 1988, 1992; Lai et al., 1992, 1994, 1995; Yin and Peng, 1995).
The Yiwagou Section lies along a ravine near Zhagana village, Tewo County (start point GPS 34.256N, 103.204E, Fig. 1).

The section is ∼1500 m long, with the highest point reaching 4060 m above sea level, and consists of continuous strata from upper Permian to Lower Triassic composed of the Changhsing Formation (P3ch), the Zhalishan Formation (T1z), and the Maresongduo Formation (T1m).
The Changhsing Formation is mostly gray, thick-bedded limestone and oolitic limestone.

The Zhalishan Formation (Griesbachian to Smithian) is 565.5m thick, consisting of gray to dark gray, thin- to mediumbedded micritic and bioclastic limestone with intercalations of calcareous, reddish to purple-red, fine-grained sandy limestone (Fig. 2).
The Maresongduo Formation (Spathian) consists of red to purple-red, thick-bedded crystallized dolomite, dolomitic limestone, and micritic limestone.
Overall, red beds first appear within the lower Zhalishan Formation and roughly increase in importance upwards.
Marine Red Beds (MRBs) are more typically found in deeper offshore environment (Song et al., 2017), but are rare in shallow-water carbonate platform settings such as the Yiwagou Section.
The MRB horizons likely record fluctuating oxygen concentration and water depth in the southern Qinling Basin (Lai et al., 1992).
hypothesis: Zhagana village, Tewo County is the location of Yiwagou Section.

The articulated shells of Late Permian Claraia (Bivalvia) specimens are commonly preserved, indicating in situ preservation.
The Late Permian deep water setting have been inherited to Early Triassic (He et al., 2015).
The sedimentary models of the Early and Middle Triassic successions in this section have been analyzed by He et al. (2015).

The lower part of the overlying Luolou Formation is characterized by yellowish, thin-bedded silty mudstones and calcareous mudstones (=beds 1–9 of He et al., 2015), which contain abundant bivalve and ammonoid fossils, while the upper part is dominated by greyish-black, thin-bedded limestones.
Beds 3, 5, 7 and 9 are composed of thin-bedded calcareous mudstones, while beds 4 and 8 are featured by thin-bedded silty mudstones.
Besides, bed 6 consists of thin-bedded muddy siltstone.
Laminations formed by deposition from suspension could be seen in beds 3–9, which indicates basinal facies succession.
However, in the study area, the lowermost part of the Luolou Formation and the Permian-Triassic boundary is not well cropped out.

premise: The well-exposed Motianling section (23°24’34"N, 107°00’18"E), which spans the uppermost Permian to lowermost Middle Triassic, is located on the margin of the Debao isolated carbonate platform in the Nanpanjiang Basin (Fig. 1).

The studied section is composed of three formations, the uppermost part of the Heshan Formation, the Luolou Formation and the basal part of the Baifeng Formation, and can be divided into four lithological units (Fig. 2).
These units are 4, 21.11, 41.42 and 7.15 m in thickness, respectively.
Unit I, the uppermost Heshan Formation, is marked by dark grey thin-bedded bioclastic limestone (Fig. 3a).
This unit contains large numbers of fusulinid and non-fusulinid foraminifers, algae, ostracods, bivalves and other marine fauna, which implies an open-marine platform environment.
The Luolou Formation is divided into two units, Unit II and Unit III. Unit II comprises thick-bedded microbialites, dolomitized limestone and oolites (Fig. 3a and b).
Microbialites in the Motianling section are thrombolytic and consist of a digitate micritic framework enclosed in sparry cement.

Because the transition from thrombolytes to oolites can be a function of deepening (Wang et al. 2019), Unit II indicates a relatively restricted platform environment with a slight overall deepening trend upwards.
Unit III comprises dark grey and reddish, medium- to thick-bedded, argillaceous limestone (Fig. 3c and d).
Together with abundant ammonoid fossils (Fig. 3e), the sedimentary facies of Unit III indicates a low-energy inter-shelf basin.
Unit IV, the lowermost Baifeng Formation, consists of claystone or sandstone (Fig. 3f ).

It should be noted that a possible hiatus is recorded between Unit I and the overlying microbialites (basal Unit II), which is also seen at the Taiping and Dajiang sections in the Nanpanjiang Basin (Jiang et al. 2014; Xiao et al. 2018; Tian et al. 2019).
hypothesis: Motianling section has latitude and longitude 23°24’34"N, 107°00’18"E.

These units are 4, 21.11, 41.42 and 7.15 m in thickness, respectively.
Unit I, the uppermost Heshan Formation, is marked by dark grey thin-bedded bioclastic limestone (Fig. 3a).
This unit contains large numbers of fusulinid and non-fusulinid foraminifers, algae, ostracods, bivalves and other marine fauna, which implies an open-marine platform environment.
The Luolou Formation is divided into two units, Unit II and Unit III. Unit II comprises thick-bedded microbialites, dolomitized limestone and oolites (Fig. 3a and b).
Microbialites in the Motianling section are thrombolytic and consist of a digitate micritic framework enclosed in sparry cement.

Because the transition from thrombolytes to oolites can be a function of deepening (Wang et al. 2019), Unit II indicates a relatively restricted platform environment with a slight overall deepening trend upwards.
Unit III comprises dark grey and reddish, medium- to thick-bedded, argillaceous limestone (Fig. 3c and d).
Together with abundant ammonoid fossils (Fig. 3e), the sedimentary facies of Unit III indicates a low-energy inter-shelf basin.
Unit IV, the lowermost Baifeng Formation, consists of claystone or sandstone (Fig. 3f ).

Member II is a 580 m platformslope facies that includes dark nodular micritic limestone, muddy limestone and arenaceous micritic limestone with bands of dolomite.

Thin-bedded micritic limestone in Bed 19 (Figure 2(b)) contains abundant vertebrate fragments and siliceous concretions.
It is therefore comparable with the bed containing the Luoping Biota at Daaozi (Figure 2(a)).
Fossiliferous strata of Member II in the Daaozi Section (Figure 2(a)) consist of 16 m of thin to moderately thick-bedded micritic limestone.

premise: The Xinmin Section is located at Xinmin valley, Puding County, Guizhou Province, South China (Fig. 1) and is easily accessible, well exposed, and displays a continuous sedimentation from the thin-bedded siliceous mudstone in the Talung Formation and mudstone in the Luolou Formation, indicating a deep water basinal facies.
Previously, primary works have been carried on the adjacent area of this section.
Yao et al. (1980) have found abundant ammonoids, gastropods, brachiopods and foraminifers at the Jiaozishan Section, which is about 4 km south to Xinmin.

Research on Guizhou stratigraphy (Dong, 1997) showed that ammonoid Pseudotirolites is common in the Talung Formation in this area, associated with brachiopods, bivalves, gastropods, trilobites and fossil plants.
Recently, many researches related to the end-Permian event were focused on the Xinmin Section.
Feng et al. (2011) first described the strata across the PTB and reported trilobite Pseudophillip sp. from the top of Changhsingian at this section.

Hu et al. (2012, 2011) found organic carbon isotope exhibited a distinct negative shift in bed 5. According to the magnetic susceptibility curve and combining with some geochemistry index, Xu et al. (2012) figured out three paleoclimatic stages across the PTB. Based on geochemistry works, Shen et al. (2013, 2012) discussed the volcanism records at this section.
Conodont biostratigraphy at this section were literally reported (without conodont image illustration, e.g., Shen et al. (2013, 2012), Xu et al. (2012), Feng et al. (2011), Hu et al. (2011).

Xu et al. (2012) have reported that Hindeodus parvus in the upper part of bed 5-3, suggesting that the PTB should be placed in bed 5-3. Unfortunately, conodonts have never been illustrated in these references leading to the PTB at the section incredible.
During the past 4 years, we carried out intensive conodont biostratigraphic works at the Xinmin Section.
Hereby, we provide the first-hand conodont data to define the PTB at this section.
This will be helpful to improve correlations among basinal sections and sections from other facies and promote the research in the basinal facies sections of the PTB.

premise: Studied P-T boundary successions were deposited across the Paleotethys ocean at tropical latitudes between 0 and 20°N (Kocsis and Scotese, 2021; Figure 2).
The studied Chibi Section (29.7515 N, 113.9519 E) is located in South China about 100 km south of the city of Wuhan (Hubei Province).
The study area is part of the South China Block which was situated in tropical latitudes at the eastern margin of the Paleotethys Ocean during the Lopingian.
At that time, the South China Block was characterized by a vast carbonate platform (Yangtze Platform) passing into a deeper basin with siliceous carbonate and chert deposition further north.

During the Wuchiapingian, the Chibi section was located on a shallow water platform, but as consequence of a relative sea level rise, the depositional setting changed to a deeper slope setting in the latest Changhsingian.
The continuous sedimentary succession is represented by the Lopingian Wujiaping and Dalong Formations as well as the Early Triassic Daye Formation.
With the depositional environment deepening during the Changhsingian, dark gray to black siliceous carbonates and cherts with sponge spicules and radiolarian tests (Dalong Formation) were deposited.
The P-T transition is characterized by a volcanic ash bed followed by thinly bedded, in part dolomitic light gray carbonates and marls of the Early Triassic (Daye Formation).
While some latest Permian and Early Triassic beds are rich in gastropods and show signs of bioturbation, most carbonates are laminated and lack fossils (Figure 3).

premise: Five sections have been logged between the Three Brothers and the White Face volcanic peaks (Fig. 1).
Section #1 is located on the western side of Hurricane Cliffs (Fig. 2a).
About 300 m away, four additional sections (#2–5) have been logged along the northern flank of Workman Wash (Fig. 2b).
Among them, section #1 provides the most complete sedimentary succession of Early Triassic deposits that cap Permian limestones of the Kaibab Formation (Figs. 3, 4).
These latter deposits correspond to a succession of dolostones, dolosiltstones, and bioclastic limestones that are more or less dolomitized, silicified, and bioturbated.
This Permian succession is interrupted by a pluri-meter thick channelized breccia interval.
Just below this conglomeratic interval, Permian limestones reveal an extensive karstification extending up to 2 m thick in this area.
A second karstified interval is observed approximately 3 m below a surface that probably represents the top of the Kaibab Formation and the Permian–Triassic transition (Fig. 4).
Above this surface, the Early Triassic sedimentary succession is approximately 70 m thick.
Unfortunately, scree slopes hide the outcrop 30 m before the Early Pleistocene basalts that cap the section (Fig. 2b).
This Early Triassic succession displays in ascending order deposits of the Rock Canyon Conglomerate, Sinbad, and Lower Red Formations.
Along section #1, deposits of the Rock Canyon Conglomerate Formation are about 17 m thick (Fig. 4).
They can be subdivided into four successive lithological units.
The first one corresponds to a first yellow clastic unit that is at least 3.5 m thick.
It is overlain by a 3-m-thick red bed unit that is itself capped by a second yellow clastic unit.
A 5-m-thick conglomeratic breccia unit marks the end of the Rock Canyon Conglomerate Formation.
Above it, the Sinbad Formation consists of a single 18-m-thick fenestral-microbial limestone unit.
A third level of yellow clastic deposits characterizes the uppermost part of the section, which is considered here to belong to the Lower Red Formation.
hypothesis: western side of Hurricane Cliffs is the location of Section #1.

premise: Mansuy (1912, 1919) and Patte (1926) studied Triassic strata containing abundant macro fossils in Lang Son, Quang Ninh, and Bac Giang Provinces, North Vietnam.

Mansuy (1912, 1919) reported many Triassic bivalves, including Avicula (=Pteria), Cassianella, Gervilleia (= Lansonella), Myophoria (= Costatoria or Neoschuzoides), and Anodontophora (=Trigonodus), from various areas in Lang Son Province.
Vu Khuc (1963) and Vu Khuc et al. (1991) redescribed some bivalve species, and additionally reported abundant Middle Triassic bivalves.
Vu Khuc (1980) and Dang (2006) described the stratigraphy of this area.

In An Chau Basin, the Triassic system is divided into the Lower Triassic Induan to Lower Olenekian Lang Son and Olenekian Bac Thuy Formations; the Middle Triassic Anisian KhonbLang, Upper Anisian Diem He, and Anisian to Ladinian Na Khuat Formations; and the Upper Triassic Mau Son Formation.

premise: The Taiping section is located 500m northeast of Taiping Town, Pingguo County, Guangxi Province (23°30′00”N; 107°31′20″E).

It was deposited in the interior of the Pingguo Platform at inferred water depths of ~10–30m (Fig. 1B; water depths may have been greater in the early to middle Late Permian as suggested by chert interbeds in the lower Heshan Formation).
It consists of medium-bedded bioclastic limestone of the Upper Permian Heshan Formation, overlain by microbialites of the Lower Triassic Majiaoling Formation (Fig. 3B).
The PTB is located at the base of the microbialites based on the first occurrence datum of H. parvus (unpublished data from Kui Wu).

Two possible erosion surfaces were noted in outcrop: the lower one located at the lithologic contact between Heshan bioclastic limestones and Majiaoling microbialites (“basal PTBM diastem”; see below), and the upper one located along a stylolite 2 cm above this contact (“lowermost Triassic diastem”; Fig. 3B).

premise: The Dongpan section is located near Dongpan Village, Liuqiao Town, Fusui County, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region (Fig. 1).

The section is situated in the southern portion of the Yangtze Basin; the sediments were deposited in the Youjiang Sub-basin during the latest Permian and earliest Triassic (Wu et al. 1994, Yin 1997).
The Dongpan section comprises the upper part of the Talung Formation and the basal part of the Luolou Formation.

The lower part (beds 2–6) of the exposed Talung Formation is characterized by cherts and fossiliferous siliceous mudstones intercalated with claystones and manganiferous limestones, yielding abundant radiolarians, brachiopods and bivalves, and the upper part (beds 7–12) by siliceous mudstones with more common intercalations of claystone.
The Talung Formation is overlain conformably by the Luolou Formation (beds 13–16), which consists mainly of yellow and yellowish green mudstones.

premise: During the Early Jurassic, the area that is now western Alberta was the easternmargin of the Panthalassa Ocean, part of theWestern Canada Sedimentary Basin (Fig. 1).

Marine Lower Jurassic strata of the Fernie Formation crop out in the foothills of the Canadian Rockies and are particularly well exposed at the Ya Ha Tinda Ranch near Banff National Park (e.g., Frebold, 1957; Hall, 1984; Poulton and Hall, 1993; Hall et al., 1998; Asgar-Deen, 2003).

These outcrops have long been studied for biostratigraphic control (ammonites and coccolithophores) on the Fernie Formation (Hall and Howarth, 1983; Hall, 1984, 1987, 2006; Hall et al., 1998, 2000, 2004; Asgar-Deen et al., 2003, 2004; Them et al., 2017); the biostratigraphic work is complemented by a handful of U-Pb dates from zircons in Ya Ha Tinda ash beds (Hall et al., 2004).
hypothesis: Ya Ha Tinda Ranch includes the strata Fernie Formation.

premise: 2.1. Huangzhishan section The Huangzhishan section, about 40 km apart from the wellknown Meishan section (see below), is situated at the Huangzhishan town of Huzhou city, Zhejiang Province, South China (Fig. 1).
Here, the uppermost Permian comprises bioclastic limestone of the Changhsing Formation.

The top units (Beds 17–18) are constrained as a latest Changhsingian age by the Neogondella yini conodont zone, typical of the Bed 24 of the Changhsing Formation at the Meishan section (Yin et al., 2001).
This formation is capped by a thin layer of dark muddy limestone (Bed 19) rich in trace fossil Chondrites ichnosp.

The possible P/Tr mass extinction horizon is calibrated to the base of Bed 19 by the first occurrence of the conodont N. meishanensis and is also marked by dramatic drop in biodiversity that coincides with onset of anoxic event (Chen et al., 2009; Fig. 2).
The overlying Huangzhishan Formation (HF) is a 4.5-m-thick succession comprising alternation of mudstone, calcareous mudstone and muddy limestone.
Black mudstone dominates the basal part of the HF (Beds 20–21), while muddy limestone-dominated successions feature the upper part of the formation (Beds 25–30).
The common occurrence of the conodont N. meishanensis Zone suggests that Beds 19–21 correlate with Beds 25–26 of the Meishan section (Chen et al., 2004, 2009).
The first occurrence of conodont Hindeodus parvus at the base of Bed 25 marks the P/Tr boundary.
Beds 25–30 are constrained as an earliest Griesbachian (early Induan) in age by the H. parvus Zone and these beds are rich in benthic faunas.

premise: 2.2. Meishan section The Meishan section, located at the Meishan town of Changxing county, Zhejiang Province, South China is the Global Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) of the PTB (Yin et al., 2001).
Here, the latest Permian Changhsing Formation comprises limestone.
The lowest Triassic Yinkeng Formation is dominated by greenish mudstone at the lower part and by thin-bedded limestone at the upper part.
The P/Tr boundary is placed at the middle part of Bed 27 and marked by the first occurrence of conodont Hindeodus parvus (Yin et al., 2001; see also Fig. 2).
The end-Permian mass extinction is calibrated to the base of Bed 25 (Jin et al., 2000) or at 1–2 cm below top of Bed 24 (Kaiho et al., 2006).
Xie et al. (2005) recognized another possible extinction horizon at the base of Bed 28 at Meishan.
Shelly communities documented here came from the uppermost Changhsing Formation (Bed 24) and throughout the entire Yinkeng Formation (Fig. 2).
Bed 24 is defined by the N. yini Zone of latest Changhsingian age (Yin et al., 2001).
Beds 25–26 are constrained by the N. meishanensis conodont zone.
Bed 27 is defined by the first occurrence of H. parvus at its middle part, marking the beginning of the Triassic.

Apart from the H. parvus Zone, the Isarcicella staeschei-I. isarcica and Neogondolella tulongensis-N. carinata conodont zones are proposed by Zhang et al. (2007) for Beds 28–51 and Beds 52–62, respectively (Fig. 2).

premise: The Shangsi section is located about 1 km north of the Shangsi Village, Guangyuan City, Sichuan Province, and its sequence is very well exposed along the Changjianggou Creek.
The section was located in the eastern Paleotethys and near the paleoequator during the Lopingian, and was previously assigned to the Equatorial Warm Water Province (EWWP; Mei and Henderson, 2001).
Sediments were deposited in a slope to basinal setting on the northwest margin of the South China Block during the Lopingian (Fig. 1).
Although strata of the entire Permian are well exposed here, this study mainly focuses on the Wuchiaping, Talung and the base of the Feixianguan formations.
The Wuchiaping Formation is subdivided into the Wangpo Shale at the base and the main part comprising limestone.

The Wangpo Shale is composed of limonite, silty mudstone, coal and ash beds, and is up to 2 m thick; it was deposited and exposed during the lowstand that led to the development of a major unconformity in many other regions (Mei, 1995; Mei and Shi, 1999; Mei et al., 1999; Shi et al., 1999).
Most of the Wuchiaping Formation is composed of medium- to thick-bedded limestone with cherty nodules.
The Talung Formation consists of thin-bedded limestone with cherty nodules in the lower part, organic-rich limestone in the middle part, and siliceous limestone with many ash beds in the upper part.

The basal Feixianguan Formation is composed of calcareous mudstone interbedded with argillaceous limestone in the basal part, followed by thin-bedded limestone with debris flow deposits higher in the section.

premise: The Guryul Ravine Section lies in the northernmost Indian state of Kashmir [72](Fig 4), the geology of which has been extensively reviewed by by Nakazawa et al. [27], Kapoor [1]and Tewari et al [36].

During the Late Permian and Early Triassic, the Kashmir region of the Indian sub-continent was located in northern Gondwana, at 35°S palaeolatitude along the southern margin of the Tethys Sea [73,74].

The depositional setting of the Late Permian Zewan Formation was a shallow marine environment with relatively high terrigenous sediment supply, whereas the Early Triassic Khunamuh Formation was deposited during a transgressive episode [74].
Marine sediments of the Guryul Ravine accumulated above pre-existing volcanic rocks [1].
Isotopic evidence of Proemse et al., 2013 [75] indicates relatively oxic conditions in the shallow marine regions of the Northwest margin of Pangea throughout the Late Permian Mass Extinction (LPME).

However, the organic carbon flux study of Algeo et al., 2013 [76], and others [74,77]on the PTB sections have suggested that the well-oxygenated conditions were briefly interrupted by periods of anoxia in the Late Permian-Early Triassic shallow marine environments.

The Guryul Ravine Section represents a continuous gradational sequence across the PT Boundary, whereas depositional hiatuses present in other Kumaon and Spiti Himalayas sections preclude a continuous record of paleoenvironmental changes during the PT Boundary Event.
Our study of organic matter at the Guryul Section [36], reveals the prevalence of amorphous organic matter (AOM), which perhaps suggests a regional prevalence of anoxic conditions.
Stratigraphically, both the Zewan and Khunmuh Formations have been further sub-divided into members and units, respectively, based on lithological and paleontological characteristics.
The Zewan Formation is divided into four Members (A-D) [1](Fig 2).

Carbonate rocks and sandy shale comprise Member A, Member B is shale with low carbonate content, Member C is thick bedded sandy limestone, sandy shale and muddy sandstone, and Member D is calcareous muddy sandstone.
Only Members A, C and D are rich in marine fossils.
An abrupt change in sedimentation to intercalated grey to black limestone and black shale demarcates the onset of the Khunamuh Formation.
This Formation is divided in to six members E-J (Fig 2), with the lower units in Member E marking the PT Boundary Event.
Member E is sub-divided into Units E1,E2 and E3. The Unit E1 contains mixed faunal elements of Late Permian and Early Triassic age.
The PT Boundary has been placed at the base of the conodont Hindeodus parvus zone at the contact of E1 and E2 (Fig 2).

We also found evidence for oxygenated conditions.

The termination of the positive isotope excursion indicates the transition from the Griesbachian Mazzin Member to the Siusi Member of the Werfen Formation at Uomo (Fig. 2) (Horacek et al., 2007).

premise: The Dajiang section in Guizhou Province, South China, preserves a detailed record of depositional conditions on a shallow-marine carbonate platform in the southern SCB during the Permian-Triassic.
The section exposes one of several isolated shallow-marine carbonate platforms that together comprise the Great Bank of Guizhou (Lehrmann et al., 1998).

The Upper Permian part mainly comprises skeletal packstones belonging to the Wuchiaping Formation, which yields diverse fusulinid and non-fusulinid foraminifers, corals, sponges, bryozoans, gastropods, brachiopods and calcareous algae (Lehrmann et al., 2003; Song et al., 2009; Lehrmann et al., 2015).
This assemblage suggests that well-oxygenated, warm, tropical shallow-marine conditions persisted in the run-up to the mass extinction.
The top surface of the packstone unit is marked by hollows fifilled by a wackestone that yields the basal Triassic conodont Hindeodus parvus (Jiang et al., 2014).

This irregular surface has been ascribed to erosion and karstifification (Liu et al., 2007; Collin et al., 2009; Wignall et al., 2009) or alternatively to submarine dissolution (Payne et al., 2007; Lehrmann et al., 2015).

The Wuchiaping Formation is overlain by ~14 m of microbialites belonging to Daye Formation that rests directly on the packstones, or in places on the hollow-fifilling wackestones of the Wuchiaping Formation.
The MEB is placed at this formational contact.

premise: To test this hypothesis, detailed pyrite framboid data was collected from a P/Tr deep-water section (Changtanhe section) from South China, and the results of this study confifirm an oxygenation event indeed occurred for a short interval after the end-Permian mass extinction.
The study area is situated in Cili County, about 200 km northwest of the capital city (Changsha) of Hunan province, South China (Fig. 1A).
Permian to Middle Triassic carbonate rocks are well exposed in this area (Fig. 1B).
Regional paleogeographic research shows that there was topographic highland ranging from Liulinpu to Cili County during the Late Permian.

A carbonate platform edged with sponge reefs developed along the northern margin of the topographic highland (Wang et al., 1997), which pass northward into siliceous limestone or radiolarian chert that were deposited in a deep shelf depositional environment (Fig. 1C).

Pyrite framboid analysis was conducted on samples from the Changtanhe section, which cuts across the uppermost Permian (Changhsingian) Dalong Formation and lowermost Triassic (Griesbachian) Daye Formation (Fig. 2).

The Upper Permian Dalong Formation (Changhsingian) is mainly comprised of dark-gray laminated wackestone that includes siliceous nodules or bands; thin-bedded mudstone and clay beds become more common towards the top of the Dalong Formation.
Thin section analysis reveals abundant radiolarians, non-fusulind foraminifers, sponge spicules and echinoderm fragments (see Fig. 2A, B).

premise: We investigated the chemostratigraphy of two sections on the Yangtze Platform spanning the Upper Ordovician and Ordovician–Silurian boundary (OSB).

The first is the Wangjiawan section in northern Yichang of western Hubei Province, which was deposited in a deep-shelf setting on the central Yangtze Block that had relatively unrestricted watermass exchange with the open ocean to the northwest (Fig. 1B).

The second is the Nanbazi section at Honghuayuan of Tongzi in northern Guizhou Province, which was deposited in the interior of the Yangtze Sea, about ~500 km to the southwest of the Wangjiawan section (Fig. 1B).
This section was located in a sub-basin in the innermost part of the shelf and, thus, had a potentially strongly restricted watermass.
Water depths at both sites are estimated at ~100–150 m, although Nanbazi may have been somewhat shallower than Wangjiawan (Chen, 1984).

The study sections have been the subject of earlier bio-, chrono-, and chemostratigraphic studies (Mu et al., 1981; Chen, 1984; Chen et al., 1987, 2000a; Yan et al., 2009), providing a high-resolution framework for the present study.

The two study sections exhibit similar stratigraphic successions, comprising the Upper Ordovician Wufeng and Kuanyinchiao formations and the lower Silurian Lungmachi Formation (Fig. 2; Chen and Rong, 1991; Chen et al., 2001; Zhan and Jin, 2007).
The Wufeng Formation consists of dark-gray, yellowish–green, and light purplish–gray, microthin to thin-bedded, quartz-silty argillaceous rocks containing local concentrations of organic matter.

It contains few benthic fauna but a continuous succession of extraordinarily well-preserved graptolites as a result of deposition in anoxic deep waters (Sun, 1931; Zhang et al., 1964; Mu et al., 1981; Wang et al., 1993).
The Kuanyinchiao Formation, which is characterized by the Hirnantia Fauna, is also known as the Kuanyinchiao Bed in many Chinese publications.

It consists of dark gray to yellowishgray, thin-bedded siliceous rocks, calcirudite debris flows, and limestone turbidites that record lowstand conditions during the Hirnantian glacial maximum (Rong, 1984; Rong et al., 2002; Chen et al., 2006; Fan et al., 2009).
The overlying Lungmachi Formation is subdivided into two units.
The lower unit (“black shale member”) is composed of black, graptolite-rich siliceous and carbonaceous shales, representing the interval of rising sea levels following the Hirnantian glacial maximum.
The upper unit (“yellow–green shale member”) is composed of lighter-colored shale, sandy shale, and siltstone, representing stable sea levels following the termination of Hirnantian glaciation.

premise: The Dongpan section (22°16.196′N, 107°41.505′E) is located between the villages of Dongmen and Liuqiao in Fusui County, Guangxi Province (Fig. 1B).
It represents a deep basinal environment with water depths of ,200–500 m (He et al., 2005, 2007a, 2007b; Feng et al., 2007).
This section contains the upper part of the upper Permian Dalong Formation and the basal part of the Lower Triassic Luolou Formation (Fig. 2).
The Dalong Formation is subdivided into 12 beds.

Beds 1–5 consist of chert and siliceous mudstone containing abundant siliceous sponge spicules and radiolarians as well as some brachiopods, bivalves, ammonoids, forminifers, and ostracodes (He et al., 2005, 2007a, 2007b; Feng et al., 2007).
These beds have been assigned to the Neoalbaillella optima Zone of late Changhsingian age (Jin et al., 2007).

Bed 6 is a bentonite containing a few radiolarians and siliceous sponge spicules, whereas Beds 7–12 consist of siliceous mudstone and silty mudstone containing abundant ostracodes, brachiopods, ammonoids, and bivalves, as well as some radiolarians and siliceous sponge spicules.
These beds are regarded as latest Changhsingian in age on the basis of agediagnostic ammonoids, conodonts, and radiolarians (Bu et al., 2006; Feng et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2008; Wu and Feng, 2008).

The end-Permian extinction horizon is located within Bed 9. Bed 13, the base of the Luolou Formation, consists of yellow silty mudstone and has been assigned an early Induan (earliest Triassic) age because it contains the age-diagnostic bivalves Claraia dieneri, C. griesbachi, C. hunanica, and C. cf. wangi, as well as the ammonoid Ophiceras sp. (Bu et al., 2006).
Both the bivalve and ammonoid faunas have been correlated to other sections in South China (e.g., Meishan GSSP, Chen et al., 2009, 2010).

premise: The Ganxi section (31°54.302′ N, 104°41.643′ E) is located at Ganxi town in central Sichuan Province.
Geologically it belongs to the Longmenshan region, the north-western margin of the Upper Yangtze Plate.
This section is one of the most typical marine Devonian sections in China (Fig. 1).
The Devonian strata of this section are well exposed along the Pingtonghe River, between Guixi and Shawozi village of Jiangyou city (Li et al., 2016).

The Givetian-Famennian sequence in this section is up to 1000 m thick, in ascending order, including the Guanyinqiao, Tuqiaozi, Shawozi, Xiaolingpo, and Maoba formations (Hou, 1988; Chen, 1994; Zhang and Gong, 2010; Zhang et al., 2016) (Fig. 2).

The Guanwushan Formation is mainly composed of medium- and thick-bedded micrite limestone, bioclastic limestone, dolomitic limestone, and dolomite, most likely representing open to restricted platform environments (Zhang et al., 2016).
It contains abundant fossils, such as coral, stromatoporoid, bryozoan, and brachiopod and dated as late Givetian in age.
The Tuqiaozi Formation, which is early Frasnian in age, conformably overlies the Guanwushan Formation and is composed of micrite and muddy limestone with parallel lamination.
The lower part of the Tuqiaozi Formation was deposited in open carbonate platform, while the upper part was in storm-affected ramp environments (Hou, 1988; Zhang et al., 2016).
The overlying Xiaolingpo Formation, which is of the middle Frasnian age, consists of bioclastic limestone and laminar algal limestone.
It is distinguished by a thick-bedded oncolite limestone at its base and thick-bedded calcareous dolomite at the top.
The covered Shawozi is mainly composed of dolomite with thin-bedded limestone in the lower-middle part and is late Franian to early Famennian in age.
Very rare fossils occur in this formation.
The Xiaolingpo and Shawozi formations are of lagoon facies and sometimes evaporated tidal flat facies.

The Maoba Formation conformably overlies the Shawozi Formation, and mainly comprises oolitic limestone interbedding with bioclastic limestone and laminar algal limestone, indicating intertidal grain to tidal flat environments.

premise: The Kap Stosch section was deposited in a rift basin on the embayed northern margin of Pangea (Fig. 1A).
The rapidly subsiding basin accumulated sediments at rates up to ~800 m Myr−1 at water depths of ~100–300 m (Fig. 2A).
The Upper Permian Foldvik Creek Formation consists of limestone and shale deposits from which the ammonoid Cyclolobus was recovered (Teichert and Kummel, 1976).

The Lower and Middle Permian are represented by the Johnston Canyon Formation and Ranger Canyon Formation, comprising cherts deposited in a productive continent-margin upwelling system (Schoepfer et al., 2012).

premise: The Wuhe section (N 26°45′93.6″, E 108°25′0.5″) in Guizhou Province crops out along the Qingshui River in Taijiang County.
The section includes the Doushantuo (120 m), the Dengying (12 m), and the Liuchapo (40 m) formations and a few meters of the basal Niutitang Formation (Figs 1D and 2).
The Doushantuo Formation can be divided into four distinct members (Members I–IV) that are roughly correlatable with those in the Yangtze Gorges area (Fig. 1D; Jiang et al., 2011).

The base of the Doushantuo Formation consists of a 2.3-m-thick cap carbonate (Member I) that overlies the glacial diamictite of the Nantuo Formation and serves as a marker for regional stratigraphic correlation (Jiang et al., 2006).
The top of the Doushantuo Formation is characterized by 5-m-thick, organic-rich black shales with sparse fifist-sized phosphatic-pyrite nodules (Member IV).
This black shale interval is also a distinctive marker across the Ediacaran Yangtze platform and is correlatable with the Member IV black shales in the Yangtze Gorges area.

The majority of the Doushantuo Formation consists of laminated black shales with subordinate micritic or microcrystalline dolostone and a few layers of olistostrome dolostone breccias (Members II and III).

In the middle of the Doushantuo Formation, a thick (2.5–4 m) dolostone breccia layer may record a regional stratigraphic discontinuity that has been tentatively correlated across the Yangtze platform (Jiang et al., 2007, 2011).
This interval also marks the Member II and III boundary (Figs 1D and 2) in this section.
The 12-m-thick Dengying Formation in this section is composed of micritic-microcrystalline dolostone with lenticular chert beds or nodules.
This unit is most likely time-equivalent to the lowermost portion (Hamajing Member) of the Dengying Formation in the Yangtze Gorges area (Jiang et al., 2007, 2011; Zhu et al., 2007).

The overlying Liuchapo Formation, which consists of 40-m-thick bedded cherts with thin black shale interbeds, is overlain by phosphatic organic-rich black shales of the Niutitang Formation (or Jiumenchong Formation in local stratigraphic terms).
Only a few meters of the basal Niutitang Formation is continuously exposed in this section.
There are sponge spicules and trilobites in the Niutitang confifirming a Cambrian age.

The Dian-Qian-Gui Basin (also termed as Hunan-Guizhou-Guangxi Basin) was a deep-marine embayment in the southern margin of the Yangtze plate, and experienced tectonic extension during the Early and Middle Permian (Lehrmann et al., 2007; Yin et al., 2014).

The Talung Formation consists of bedded carbonates, pyroclastic sandstones, and terrigenous siliciclastic rocks (including sandstone and marlstone).

premise: Late Permian Changhsingian time was an important time for reef-building episode in South China with east Sichuan and Chongqing in the northern part of the SCB being the most important regions for reef carbonates.
Laolongdong section located in the northwest part of Chongqing Municipality is representative of Late Permian reef facies in this area (Reinhardt, 1988; Fan et al., 1990).

Sponge-dominated reefs reach 2 km in diameter and 160 m-thick (Qiang et al., 1985), overlain by several metres of skeletal limestone (Changxing Formation) containing fusulinid and non-fusulinid foraminifers, brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids, calcareous algae, Tubiphytes and calcisponges.
The skeletal limestone is sharply overlain by a unit of 2.4 m-thick microbialite (Fig. 1B, C).
The contact between the skeletal limestone and the microbialite represents a sharp change in lithology, and corresponds to the end-Permian mass extinction event horizon (Fig. 1C).
The microbialite is overlain by poorly fossiliferous laminated mudstone of the Feixianguan Formation of Lowest Triassic (Fig. 1B).
hypothesis: Laolongdong section includes the strata Changxing Formation.

premise: We studied one such deep-water carbonate-dominant sequence at Chaotian (Latitude 32°37′N, Longitude 105°51′E), about 20 km to the north of Guangyuan city in northern Sichuan or about 60 km to the northeast of the above-mentioned Shangsi section (Fig. 1A).

This section displays continuous stratigraphy from the Middle Permian to lowermost Triassic in excellent exposures along a narrow gorge (Mingyuexia) of the Jialingjiang River, a branch of the Changjiang River (Figs. 1A, B and 2).

The overall biostratigraphy of the Chaotian section was originally clarifified on the basis of fusulines, conodonts and ammonoids (Zhao et al., 1978; Yang et al., 1987).
Later, from the viewpoint of the two Permian mass extinctions,Isozaki et al. (2004, 2007b) re-investigated the stratigraphy of this section in higher resolution.

More data on lithostratigraphy (Isozaki et al., 2008; Lai et al., 2008), fossils (fusulines, ammonoids, radiolarians, conodonts; Xu, 2006; Ji et al., 2007; Kuwahara et al., 2007, 2008; Isozaki et al., 2008; Lai et al., 2008), chemostratigraphy (carbon isotopes; Lai et al., 2008), and radiometric ages (SHRIMP U–Pb zircon ages; He et al., 2007) were also added recently.
At Chaotian, we mapped on the eastern bank of the gorge that corresponds to the south limb of the E–W trending anticline (same as the ‘Chaotian section’ by Isozaki et al., 2004; Fig. 1B).
In this study, we also used fresh rock samples for analysis, which were obtained by deep drilling at Chaotian.

As to the Permian–Triassic strata at Chaotian, we adopt the overall stratigraphic framework by Yang et al. (1987) and Isozaki et al. (2004, 2007b) including their stratigraphic subdivision and unit names.

The Permo–Triassic rocks at Chaotian consist of the Guadalupian Maokou Formation, the Lopingian Wujiaping and Dalong Formations, and the lowermost Triassic Feixianguan Formation, in ascending order (Fig. 2).

The Maokou Formation, over 200 m thick, is mainly composed of dark gray bioclastic limestone (packstone) partly containing black chert nodules, and yields abundant shallow-marine fossils, such as calcareous algae, ostracodes, and fusulines.
The topmost part of the Maokou Formation, ca. 11 m thick, is composed of bedded black calcareous mudstone and black chert with ammonoids, small-sized brachiopods, radiolarians, and conodonts.
The Wujiaping Formation, ca. 70 m thick, is mainly composed of dark gray bioclastic limestone (packstone) partly containing black chert nodules.
At the base of the Wujiaping Formation, however, a ca. 2 m thick unique non-carbonate bed called the Wangpo bed occurs.
Bioclastic packstone of the Wujiaping Formation contains shallow-marine fossils including brachiopods, calcareous algae, and conodonts.
The Dalong Formation, ca. 26 m thick, is mainly composed of black mudstone and limestone (lime mudstone/wackestone), and contains conodonts and ammonoids.
The Feixianguan Formation, over 30 m thick, is mainly composed of thinly bedded dark gray marl and light gray limestone (lime mudstone), and yields few conodonts, ammonoids, and brachiopods.

premise: The Ubara section is located at 35.189896 N, 135.2515E, near the village of Ubara in the Ayabe area (Kyoto Prefecture) of central Japan (Kimura et al., 1989).

The section is nearly flat-lying although cut by faults at several levels; samples for the present study were collected from a portion of the outcrop that was fault-free and consisted of a conformable succession of beds straddling the Permian–Triassic boundary (Kuwahara et al., 1991; Yamakita et al., 1999).

premise: The Kennecott Point section is located on the western coast of Graham Island, the northern major island of the Haida Gwaii (Fig. 2; Longridge et al., 2007).

The lowermost 12 m of the section (Fig. 3) is assigned to the Norian Peril Formation, which consists of bituminous calcareous shale and siltstone containing abundant concentrations of the flat bivalve genus Monotis (Ward et al., 2004).

The majority of the section (128 m) belongs to the Sandilands Formation (Tipper et al., 1991), which is composed of organic-rich silicified siltstones and shales, with interbeds of fine turbiditic and thin tuffaceous sandstones.
This unit ranges in age from the earliest Rhaetian to the latest Sinemurian (Longridge et al., 2007).
